I was reading about the firewall discussion in the thread here. As far as I know it's turned off by default with wepages saying that there are no connections present in a vanilla install, so it's not needed to be turned on. I was also told I didn't need a firewall on in Linux because my router has one, by a friend. Would running these commands have any benefits or drawbacks if I just mainly surf the web and have a local network?

sudo ufw enable

sudo ufw default deny

I'm using Xubuntu 15.10 on a Laptop and Desktop
Do I need to turn the firewall on in Linux?

I've used these before while running a small local network and it didn't negatively affect any of that working or browsing. You're probably safe with your router firewall protecting your network from incoming unsolicited connections but as a second layer on each computer this doesn't hurt anything either as far as as I know.

You're router is mostly likely is a Linux firewall, capable of handling abuse from the Internet's worst. A Linux desktop is using the exact same software.

More important than turning on the firewall is enabling updates, and turning off un-used services. Do you need to have a printer server running all the time? disable cups, disable avahi if zeroconf isn't used on your network, same for windows shares, samba. If no one is listening, you don't need to block things that wont happen.

The Linux firewall in the end only does one thing. It's sorta the "Unix-Way", do one thing well. It just monitors network access. So as long as you only used network programs that are updated, the firewall isn't going to help as much. It would still be required to allow used software access to the Internet, hence doing very little.

The easy way for you to do this is to download and install gufw from the repository.

The Ubuntu firewall is called iptables. I can tell you from experience it is a bitch to work with.

Someone wrote a CLI front end for iptables called "ufw" or "ultimate fire wall." It is also annoying, but a huge improvement.

Someone wrote a GUI front end for ufw called "gufw". It is awesome. It is basically idiot proof. You only need a vague idea of what a firewall is to learn how to use it.

You should configure the firewall if you set up an SSH server, a VPN server, or an FTP server.

Your router probably blocks most connections that aren't http connections. If you need to "let in" a port from the outside, you'll have to configure your router to "port forward" that port.

Example: I installed openssh-server. As a result, port 22 became activated and ready to accept ssh packets. I told my router to route all incoming traffic on port 7765 to my server's IP address at port 22. From now on, packets to my external IP address on port 7765 will be relayed to my server on port 22. If those packets are ssh packets, an ssh handshake will be attempted. I can use gufw to quickly block port 22 on my server if I'm not going to be using it.

In the other thread we were talking about building a router using a Open Source OS.

A router is something that directs your packets of information of where to go. OSI MODEL

There is some concern that the NSA may have built backdoors into most routers. Cisco is one of the most common routers in the US

Do you need a Linux router? No.

Is it fun and informative to build one? Yes.

What you need to understand is there are ports on networked computers. These are logical ports not physical ports these are not connected by an extra connection but are logical constructions used for different protocols to communicate on a network.

Only allowing traffic that you permit is an important competent of firewalls while blocking other intrusive ports or methods of access is a feature of firewalls.

Are you safe enough from most attacks using a standard router and firewall? Yes, more or less.

For a home user the chances are much smaller that someone will make a concerted attempt to break into your network than for, say, a huge multinational banking concern. But the risk is always there. Remember that firewalls and routers are just software, and software can never be 100% secure. So you decide how exposed you are and what level of security you're comfortable with. The level of protection provided by a entry level $40 router is probably a joke if it works at all, and to put your modem in Pass Through mode would the same as leaving your front door open and putting up a sign that says "Thieves Welcome". But higher end routers by recognized manufacturers provide IMO a good level of protection for the average home user and there is no need to set up a separate firewall and DMZ.

If you do want to build a firewall however then the rule of thumb is that's ALL that PC does because every piece of software that is running is a potential security hole. So slap a 2nd NIC in that old PC that's been gathering dust in the corner since 2009 and off you go. Or do it as a VM since for a typical home user the actual processing power that will be required is probably pretty small.
Always use a firewall for connection to the internet.
